name: PT Dharma Satya Nusantara Tbk

frontmatter.title: Dharma Satya Nusantara: an estate priced for a weaker palm price than the deck
frontmatter.summary: DSNG trades at 4.1x forward operating EBITDA and 7.1x forward earnings. A palm price deck that still rises, a cost base set by the audited accounts and net debt at half a year of EBITDA support a twelve-month value of Rp2,698, a total return of 107.4% from the Rp1,325 price. Rating BUY.
thesis: The DCF leg is worth Rp2,993 a share and carries 60% of the weight; the two market-based legs are worth Rp2,165 and Rp1,181 because they capitalise one year of EBITDA and a balance-sheet book. We publish the blend rather than the DCF alone, and section five says what that does to the bear case [S3, S4].

The market pays 4.1x forward operating EBITDA for an estate whose cash cost per tonne is set by the audited accounts, whose net debt is half a year of EBITDA and which owns a stake carried at book [S2, S3].
Volume is the swing factor this year: nine-month CPO production of 451 kt ran below the prior year and the company projects 1.0% output growth for the full year [F34, F60] [S4, S5].
At the Rp1,325 price the market discounts a palm price of US$1,044/t, or 84.2% of the deck's next-year level, on our cost base and our cost of capital [S0, S3].
The bear case values the shares at Rp820, below the price, and most of it is the two cross-check legs rather than the DCF; the base and bull cases carry the asymmetry [S3, S6].

catalysts.event: Fourth amendment to PP 36/2023: conversion of DHE SDA proceeds from the reksus account raised from half to full, still in preparation with no effective date
Monthly export duty and levy reset, and the December reference price
Audited accounts for the year to December and the dividend proposal
Annual general meeting and dividend approval

blocks.text: This note corrects the previous update, prices the export-proceeds relaxation, and re-derives two assumptions. The previous note said "no value change" while the published target had fallen from the initiation level by a little over one per cent. That was wrong twice: the number moved, and the stated cause — a spot exchange-rate move of a fraction of one per cent — cannot produce it. The bridge is arithmetic. The DCF leg was unchanged between the two published versions; the whole of the fall came from the two market-based legs, whose peer multiples were refreshed on the same 6 November price date as the data pack. The Indonesian peer median EV/EBITDA gave back about half a turn, with SMAR's own trailing multiple roughly halving, SGRO's falling by a sixth and FAPA's by a fifth, which took the blended EV/EBITDA multiple from about six and two-thirds to six and a third; the peer P/BV median fell by a similar fraction. The exchange rate is not the cause of that move, and it is treated below as what it is — the live channel for the new policy [S0, S3].

We maintain BUY with a twelve-month value of Rp2,698 per share, a total return of 107.4% from the Rp1,325 price, of which 103.6% is price appreciation and the balance the next-twelve-month dividend. The company is a mid-sized Indonesian oil-palm estate with a wood-products business and a small renewables arm. At the price the market capitalisation is IDR14,044.8bn and enterprise value is 4.1x our FY2026E operating EBITDA of IDR3,982.3bn, against a peer-and-history multiple of 6.3x [S0, S3, F44].

The policy event is the planned fourth amendment to PP 36/2023, which would raise from 50.0% to 100.0% the share of natural-resource export proceeds (DHE SDA) held in the special reksus account that an exporter may convert to rupiah; it is still under preparation with no effective date [S9, S10]. Its direct reach on DSNG is narrow: the palm segment sold its entire nine-month line of IDR8,059.2bn into the domestic market with nil export sales, so the palm obligation sits with the refinery buyers [S2, F61]. The export line that could be in scope is IDR977.3bn — wood products IDR824.7bn, renewables IDR152.6bn — against group revenue of IDR9,109.8bn [S2, F72, F75, F76].

Whether those proceeds are SDA exports is the question that decides if the policy touches DSNG at all, and the announcement does not settle it [S10]. Even if the whole line were in scope the effect is a carry, not a margin: at the 2.3% the model credits on cash, converting the freed balance to rupiah is worth a rounding error against EBITDA. The channel that does matter is the exchange rate, and the government's stated aim is rupiah stability [S10]. DSNG sells in dollars and costs in rupiah, so each one per cent of rupiah strength costs about two per cent of the target [S0, S3]. We keep the base unchanged because no effective date or size is announced, but we name the sign and the magnitude rather than calling the policy neutral.

Two assumptions changed. The current-year realisation ratio is now derived from the nine-month segment accounts at 0.76 of the benchmark, not fitted to land the year's EBITDA on the nine-month line; FY2026E EBITDA of IDR3,982.3bn is an output, and the run-rate comparison the previous note offered as independent corroboration has been removed [S2, F34]. The realisation legs in the scenarios widened to seven per cent — the size of the November levy move — and section five says why [S6, F77, F36]. Capex stays at the last actual's ratio to D&A, whose replanting arithmetic section three sets out [S3, F11].

DSNG is an integrated oil-palm producer. At the last year end it managed 111,900 ha planted hectares, split between nucleus estates it owns and plasma blocks it develops and supervises for smallholders, with mills concentrated in East, Central and West Kalimantan [S4, F38]. It sells CPO, palm kernel and palm kernel oil, runs a wood-products business making engineered flooring and panels from plants in Central Java, and a renewables business exporting palm-kernel shells and wood pellets to Japan and Korea [S4, S7].

The palm segment contributed 88.0% of the nine-month revenue of 9,110 IDR bn, and the export line discussed above is almost entirely the other two segments [S2, S7, F54, F31]. The palm business is therefore the valuation; wood and renewables are carried at a blended margin inside other revenue rather than as separate businesses [S3]. In the last full year CPO production reached 631 kt, sales 629 kt, fresh fruit bunch production 2,189 kt and the extraction rate 23.3% [S4, F23, F1, F25, F26]. The company printed a production target of 651 kt for that year, which the realisation missed, and projects 1.0% growth for the current year on its own budget — a growth rate, not a tonnage [S4, F46, F60]. The nine-month outturn of 451 kt makes even that look ambitious [S5, F34].

The strategy is unglamorous: replant older blocks, finish the plasma programme, delever and add small downstream projects such as a bio-CNG plant that uses mill effluent [S4, S7]. There is no large acquisition in the plan and no new planting frontier, so the capital-allocation question is whether the dividend and the replanting budget can both be funded from operating cash flow; at the last actual they could [S3, F50]. The company is controlled by the Triputra and Oetomo families, who hold 30.6% and 29.2% respectively, and the president director is a member of the Oetomo family, so this is a family-controlled mid-cap rather than a widely held corporate [S4, F55, F56].

The group holds its mills and estates through operating subsidiaries, holds an indirect stake in an associated estate in East Kalimantan and reports a small non-controlling interest [S2, S3, F44]. There is no dual-class structure and no material pledge disclosed, which is what one wants from a family-controlled name before looking at the cash flows [S4, S2].

The palm price is the single largest driver of earnings. The house deck runs CPO from US$1,007/t in the last actual year to US$1,135/t this year and US$1,240/t next, then fades to US$1,150/t in the long run [S0]. The shape matters more than the level: the deck expects the current tightness to peak next year and ease thereafter as wider-industry plantings produce. Our model takes that path as given and translates it into rupiah through the realisation ratio and the exchange rate, which is where the company-specific judgement sits [S3, S4].

The supply side is genuinely tight. GAPKI expects Indonesian output to fall by 2,200 kt in 2027 as the full effect of the long dry spell lands, and its chairman has said that reduction accounts for the complete El Nino impact rather than a partial one [S8, F37]. The company's own experience is consistent: fresh fruit bunch production fell to 1,500 kt in the first nine months, with the third quarter down on the second, and CPO output to 451 kt [S5, S7, F35, F34]. A supply decline of that size in the world's largest producer is why the deck does not fade back to the last cycle's average [S8].

The levy setting is where the arithmetic is done monthly. The Ministry of Trade sets a reference price and derives an export duty and levy from it; for November the reference price is US$979/t and the combined charge is US$246/t, down a fifth on October's US$308/t [S6, F48, F36, F77]. The same release shows the reference price falling at the same time, so net export parity — the reference price less the charge — was essentially unchanged: exporters kept a larger share of a lower price. The pair also sizes the upside branch: a charge that fell by a fifth against a stable reference price would widen parity by about sixty dollars a tonne, or seven per cent of the realised price, which is why the bull case now carries a seven per cent realisation leg rather than five [S6, F36, F77].

For a domestic seller such as DSNG, whose whole palm line is sold locally with no export sales [S2, F61], the relevant variable is the domestic price relative to the world benchmark, and the levy affects it only through that parity. The biodiesel mandate is the other pillar: the government confirmed in early November that it will keep the B50 blend, and palm oil use for biodiesel was 1,350 kt in August while exports rose and stocks fell [S6, F49]. A mandate absorbing a growing share of domestic production supports the domestic price and competes with exports for the same tonnes, so the levy and the mandate are best read together [S6].

Competitive positioning is about cost and certification, not market share. DSNG is a small producer against the national total and a price taker, but its cash cost per tonne is set by its own estate and mill efficiency, and its certification coverage is high across nucleus estates and mills [S4]. The estate is contiguous, the mills are close to the fruit, the extraction rate is above the industry average, and the certification stack is complete enough to sell into premium markets [S4, F26]. What it does not have is pricing power: the product is a commodity and the domestic price is set by a formula linked to the export reference price [S6]. That is why we value it on a through-cycle price rather than a multiple of spot, and why the cost side is built from the audited accounts [S3].

The market backdrop is a separate risk. MSCI is consulting on reclassifying Indonesia from emerging to standalone, and Indonesia's weight in the emerging-markets index has shrunk to a fraction of one per cent, so few global holders have an interest in opposing it [S11]. For a domestic mid-cap with a 33.1% free float that is a de-rating risk that has nothing to do with palm oil, and section five tests it rather than asserting that the discount is only about the commodity [S11, S0].

The export-proceeds rule is a balance-of-payments instrument: exporters of natural-resource products must place the foreign currency they earn in a special account with a domestic bank, and the rule limits how much of that balance may be converted into rupiah. The sectors it reaches are defined by regulation rather than by the customs code, so processed goods such as engineered flooring are a boundary case while unprocessed plantation and forestry products sit inside it.

The last audited year is the anchor. Revenue was 12,315 IDR bn, cost of revenue 8,465 IDR bn and gross profit IDR3,850.0bn [S3, F5, F7]. Cost of revenue carries D&A of 974 IDR bn, which the data pack understated by an order of magnitude, so the first adjustment is to restate depreciation to the audited note [S3, F9]. On that basis EBITDA was IDR3,814.6bn, a margin of 31.0%, and profit attributable to owners was 1,840 IDR bn [S3, F13].

Every EBITDA in this report is operating EBITDA: audited operating profit plus depreciation of fixed assets and right-of-use assets plus amortisation of bearer plants and intangibles, with the associate's profit excluded because the stake is carried in the bridge to equity value, and with no add-back of the impairment and no deduction of the biological-asset gain [S3]. The reconstruction of IDR3,814.6bn sits a fraction of a per cent above the audited IDR2,829.4bn plus IDR973.7bn. The audited reconciliation prints a higher number, IDR4,078.0bn, and the whole difference is line-by-line: operating profit IDR2,829.4bn plus D&A IDR973.7bn plus the associate's IDR168.4bn plus the IDR116.9bn impairment less the IDR10.4bn biological gain [S3, F52, F64-F67]. We keep our definition because the associate's earnings cannot sit inside the multiple while its book value also sits in the bridge, and a through-cycle measure should not add back an impairment the operating accounts carry [S3, F44].

The cost base is the most important number in the model. After deducting the cost of non-palm revenue at a normal margin, the cash cost of a tonne of CPO is about IDR8.0m this year, depreciation per tonne about IDR1.6m, and own capex per tonne about IDR1.4m [S3, F7, F9, F11]. Each is the last-actual unit value carried forward at the deck's long-run rupiah inflation anchor — the central bank's target midpoint, not the current consumer-price print. We use the anchor because a decade of cash flow should be inflated at a long-run rate and because terminal growth is set to the same anchor, so real margins stay flat; using the live print instead would take about four per cent off both the DCF leg and the target [S0, S3].

The last capex was 856 IDR bn, eighty-eight per cent of D&A, and we hold that ratio. The split shows why it is not under-replacement: fixed-asset additions against fixed-asset depreciation, and the capitalised-plantation line against bearer-plant amortisation, are different fractions, but replanting is booked at current cost while the amortisation runs on historical cost, so a rupiah of replanting replaces more than a rupiah of the charge [S3, F9, F11]. On the physical cycle, 111,900 ha planted hectares over roughly a quarter of a century is about four and a half thousand hectares a year, and the capitalised plantation line is the full programme at that rate [F38]. The plasma outlay is excluded because plasma collections in the same investing section reimburse it [S3, F11].

The nine-month figures show the cycle turning once put on the same operating basis. Revenue was 9,110 IDR bn, up slightly, and the printed EBITDA of 2,950 IDR bn was up by about the same margin [S2, F31, F33]. On our definition the nine months is operating profit of IDR2,113.5bn plus D&A of IDR733.2bn, up about a per cent year on year; the printed line is higher by the associate's IDR144.4bn and lower by the IDR41.4bn biological gain, the identical bridge to the annual note [S2, F68-F71]. Profit attributable to owners was 1,442 IDR bn, higher because finance costs fell as debt was repaid [S2, F32]. Operating cash flow of 1,912 IDR bn was lower than the prior year as the previous year's working-capital release reversed, and the company paid the 498 IDR bn dividend [S2, F41, F42].

The current-year forecast is close to the run-rate, and the price is the key judgement. We carry 615.0 thousand tonnes, a realised price of US$859.2 a tonne, revenue of IDR12,581.4bn, EBITDA of IDR3,982.3bn and earnings per share of Rp186.0 [S2, S3, S5]. The realisation ratio of 0.76 is derived from the nine-month segment revenue, the nine-month volume and the deck's exchange rate; it is not calibrated to an EBITDA line, and the current-year EBITDA is what the accounts plus the deck's prices produce [S2, F31, F34, S4]. Volume is below the company's own projection and the ratio at the low end of the bracket the exchange rate allows, so the base is the most probable case rather than a cautious one trimmed further; the caution is in the bear [S4, F60].

Next year the deck does the work. We do not hold the ratio flat: the nine-month accounts show a dollar wedge between benchmark and realised price that behaves like a levy-plus-freight amount, so we hold the wedge and let the ratio rise with the benchmark [S2, S6]. Beyond the explicit years the convention changes, and we state it: the ratio is held at its final explicit-year level, because the levy and freight that make the wedge reset with the reference price and with dollar costs, so in the terminal years the wedge escalates with the benchmark [S6, F36, F48]. Unit costs escalate with rupiah inflation, and revenue reaches IDR14,196.9bn and EBITDA IDR5,276.2bn [S0, S3]. Volume is held flat because the source the deck rests on says next year is the trough of the El Nino effect and recovery starts the year after [S8, F37, S5]. That is the assumption a reader should challenge; if the price instead stays at the current level, the bear case in section five is the relevant valuation [S6].

The balance sheet is in good shape. Forecast net debt at the current year end is IDR1,946.0bn against equity attributable to owners of 11,481 IDR bn at the last year end, and the bond repaid during the last year removed the largest single maturity [S2, S3, F15]. There is no material pension deficit, no material lease obligation outside the reported right-of-use assets and a small non-controlling interest [S2, S3]. The claims on cash are the dividend, assumed at a payout of 27.1%, and the replanting inside own capex [S3, F21].

Earnings quality covers three points. Accruals: profit less operating cash flow over average total assets is negative in both fiscal years and in the nine months, so the company converts more cash than it reports as profit, which is favourable [S3, S2, F13, F14, F32, F50, F41]. Cash conversion: operating cash flow has exceeded net profit in every period, although the multiple has fallen from its peak as working capital reversed in the nine months [S3, S2, F50, F41]. Related parties: purchases from the Daiken associate are 68.0% of raw-material purchases and the payable to it 30.0% of all trade payables, and no sales to related parties are disclosed [S2, F58, F59]. The listing is a standard main-board one with no special notation, and the one optics-class item is the land revaluation surplus of 2,585 IDR bn, which inflates book equity but not cash flow [S3, F57].

We value DSNG on a discounted cash flow as the primary method, with an EV/EBITDA cross-check and a P/BV cross-check. The DCF carries the controlling weight because the company is a price-taking commodity producer whose value is the present value of a long stream of cash flows at a through-cycle price, and a multiple applied to a single year's EBITDA would capitalise whatever point of the cycle that year happens to sit on [S3, S4]. The EV/EBITDA cross-check carries a smaller weight and the P/BV check the smallest, which is the house weighting for the plantation industry [S3].

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck and the house configuration, not from the reporting pack: a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, less the Indonesian default spread of 1.6% that the deck deducts from the domestic risk-free rate before it is used as the equity base, plus a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%, applied to an unlevered beta of 0.80 that is the house industry default rather than a regression on this stock and relevers to 0.94 at debt of 0.23 times market capitalisation [S2]. That gives a cost of equity of 12.1%. The cost of debt is 9.4% pre-tax, which is the risk-free rate plus the house corporate spread of 2.0% [S2]. That loan rate is the marginal rate and is deliberately above the 7.9% average finance cost the income statement carries, which reflects older, cheaper facilities; the marginal rate is the right one for discounting new capital [S3]. At a debt weight of 18.8% the weighted average cost of capital is 11.3% [S2]. We use a terminal growth rate of 2.5%, which is the long-run rupiah inflation in the macro deck and is consistent with a palm price that is flat in real terms after the explicit forecast [S0].

The DCF produces a value of Rp2,993 per share, with the terminal value accounting for 45.7% of enterprise value [S0, S3]. That terminal share is high but not extreme for a long-life estate, and it is the reason we test the terminal assumptions in the sensitivity table rather than treating the output as precise [S3]. The explicit forecast carries free cash flow from IDR2,292.1bn in the current year to IDR2,833.4bn in five years, as the price deck rises and then fades and the cost base escalates with inflation [S0, S3].

The two cross-checks sit below the DCF, and the gap is informative rather than alarming. The EV/EBITDA method applies a multiple of 6.3x to the last actual operating EBITDA of 3,814.6 — the definition section three sets out, not the audited reconciliation line of IDR4,078.0bn — and produces Rp2,165, -27.7% against the primary method [S3, F64]. The P/BV method applies 1.3x to pre-revaluation book equity of IDR9,862.6bn at the balance-sheet date — attributable equity less the land revaluation surplus of IDR2,585.1bn — and produces Rp1,181, -60.6% against the primary method [S2, F62, F63]. Pre-revaluation book is what the house earnings-quality card requires: the surplus (IDR2,585.1bn at the last year end, and unchanged at the balance-sheet date) is an accounting uplift of land values that never reaches cash flow, so applying the peer multiple to the revalued book would flatter this method by roughly a quarter [S3, F57, F62]. Even on the corrected base the method carries the smallest weight and is not a valuation anchor [S3]. The wide gap to the DCF is the point rather than an error: a book multiple on a mature estate cannot see the cash the palms generate between replantings, which is exactly what the discounted cash flow is there to capture, so the cross-check is read as a floor on asset value and not as a competing estimate [S3, S4]. The multiple is a point-in-cycle number, which is why it sits between the two [S3, S4].

One enterprise value, one year, one EBITDA definition: the market multiple quoted in this report is market capitalisation plus our forecast net debt for the current year of IDR1,946.0bn and the minorities, over our FY2026E operating EBITDA of IDR3,982.3bn, which is 4.1x on the forward year [S2, F44]. The numerator and the denominator are on the definition section three sets out, so no reader has to guess which EBITDA the multiple uses; applying the same multiple to the audited reconciliation line of IDR4,078.0bn would give a larger number, which is why the cross-check as struck is the stricter of the two [S3, F64]. On the September spot net debt the same equity capitalises the same earnings at a slightly higher multiple, and deducting the associate stake at book gives a lower one; we quote the forward basis because the target is a forward value, and the cross-check in the table above is struck on the last audited year's operating EBITDA, as it must be [S3, S4, F44].

The sensitivity table shows what matters. A move in the palm price passes more or less straight to the margin, while the same percentage move in volume carries a cost, and a move in the exchange rate has an effect close to a price move because the revenue is dollar-denominated and the cost is rupiah-denominated [S0, S3]. That asymmetry is the reason we treat the exchange rate as a first-order variable in section five rather than as a background assumption [S6, F47]. The grid's centre sits below the published base value because the grid re-runs the DCF with the deck's long-run price held at the shocked level, whereas the base case escalates it with rupiah inflation; read the grid for relative sensitivity, not for the absolute level [S0, S3].

The reverse DCF is the cleanest statement of the mispricing. At the current price the market is discounting a CPO price of US$1,044/t, below the deck's next-year level, on our cost base and our cost of capital [S0, S3]. In other words, the market is not assuming that the GAPKI supply decline happens; it is assuming that the price stays roughly where it is now and that the cost base does not improve [S8, F37]. If the deck is right, the shares are worth materially more than the price; if the market is right, the shares are worth the bear case, which is below the current price [S3, S6].

The bear case cuts the palm price, trims volumes, strengthens the rupiah and widens the domestic discount, and it values the shares at Rp820, below the current price [S3, S6]. That is the realistic bad outcome rather than a catastrophic one, and it is no longer a mirrored price shock: the exchange-rate and realisation legs were missing from the initiation and are the reason the bear now falls below the price. A deeper trough stress values the equity about a tenth below the bear case, at roughly a third of the base case: it cuts the palm price by a third from the deck's current-year level of US$1,135/t, takes volume and the rupiah a tenth lower each and the realisation a twentieth lower [S6, F47]. That number is floored by the two cross-checks rather than produced by the discounted cash flow: at shocks that deep the explicit free cash flow turns negative and the DCF leg drops out of the blend, so the value is carried by the EV/EBITDA method on the last actual and the P/BV method on pre-revaluation book. The stress therefore understates a true trough rather than representing one, and it is a model floor rather than a claim about the historical low: the reviewed price series in this packet runs back only a few years, so the level is labelled a stress and not a sourced cycle trough [S0, S3]. We run it separately rather than adding a fourth scenario and fold its weight into the bear probability, so the published table stays the three house cases [S3]. The same applies to the policy tail: an export-ban or DMO tightening that closes the domestic outlet is a low-probability event we describe here and do not model as a separate scenario [S6].

The base case values the shares at Rp2,769 and the bull case at Rp4,433, with probabilities of 25%, 50% and 25% respectively [S3]. The bull case carries the two upside legs the report argues: a stronger supply deficit after the GAPKI decline lifts CPO above the deck, El Nino recovery and plasma maturities add volume, the rupiah weakens and the levy-driven domestic discount narrows [S8, S4, S6]. The scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers — price, volume, exchange rate and realisation — so the asymmetry in the values comes from the operating leverage of the estate rather than from a different set of assumptions in each case [S3].

The dividend is the market's other anchor. At through-cycle free cash flow the equity generates an FCFE yield of 14.7% against a dividend yield of 3.8%, so the stated payout policy leaves a wide margin of dividend capacity that is not in the price [S3, F21]. The model's net cash build — net debt of -2,515.1 by FY2028 — is reachable as a higher payout or a special dividend rather than stranded, because the capital plan has no large expansion to absorb it [S3, S4]. A payout normalisation is close to neutral for the twelve-month total return in this model, since a larger dividend is offset by a lower ex-dividend value, but it de-risks the return and is the clearest use of the cash [S3].

The first risk is the palm price itself. A sustained fall in the dollar price, whether from a demand shock or from a larger supply response than GAPKI expects, would hit revenue directly and would also widen the domestic discount if the levy is not cut in step [S6, S8]. The second is weather. El Nino has already cut fresh fruit bunch production, and a second dry year would push the volume recovery out by a year and raise the unit cost as fixed costs spread over fewer tonnes [S5, F35]. The third is policy. The export levy, the reference price formula and the biodiesel mandate are all set administratively, and a change in any of them changes the domestic price without changing the company's cost [S6, F36, F48].

The fourth risk is the exchange rate. The rupiah was Rp18,140/USD in early November, close to its weakest on record, and while a weak rupiah helps the revenue line it also raises the rupiah cost of imported fertiliser and fuel [S6, F47]. The fifth is execution: replanting is a multi-year programme that reduces the mature area before it increases it, and a delay in the plasma programme would slow the volume recovery [S4]. The sixth is governance and related-party risk, which we discuss in the next section; the related-party balances are small, but the company is family-controlled and the associate is a related party [S2, S3, F53].

Liquidity is adequate but not deep. The average daily traded value is IDR7.5bn, the free float is 33.1%, and the shares have traded between Rp1,075.0 and Rp1,860.0 over the last year [S0]. A large holder would need patience to build or exit a position, which is a real constraint for an institutional investor even if it is not a valuation input [S0].

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A second consecutive quarter of falling fresh fruit bunch production without a price response would push us toward the bear case [S5]. A levy increase that widens the domestic discount would do the same [S6]. A decision to cut the biodiesel mandate, or a failure of the B50 programme to absorb the expected volumes, would remove the domestic demand support that the base case relies on [S6]. On the other side, a confirmed GAPKI output decline and a rising reference price would move us toward the bull case [S8, F48].

DSNG is controlled by two families. The Triputra family interests hold 30.6% and the Oetomo family interests 29.2%, with a further block held by an investment company and the remainder in public hands [S4, S3, F55, F56]. The ultimate beneficiaries named in the annual report are Ny. T.P. Rachmat L.R. Imanto and Andrianto Oetomo, and the president director is a member of the Oetomo family, so the controlling shareholders and the management are the same people [S4]. The public holds 33.1% on the exchange's free-float measure, comfortably above the minimum, and the company is not on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list [S0, S4].

The audit is clean. The consolidated accounts are audited by Siddharta Widjaja and Rekan, the Indonesian member firm of KPMG, and the opinion is unmodified in all material respects [S4, S3]. The board includes independent commissioners alongside the executive directors, and the annual report discloses the directors' shareholdings, which are concentrated in the two families [S4]. There is no dual-class share structure and no material pledge of shares disclosed [S4].

Related-party dealings are modest at the balance-sheet level. Trade payables to related parties were 2.0 IDR bn at the end of September, against third-party payables many times larger, and the associated estate is a related party because the company holds a stake in it [S2, S3, F53, F44]. The company lent to that associate in the past, but the loan was repaid in full in April 2025, so the related-party receivable is no longer a financing exposure [S3]. The share of the associate's profit is disclosed separately and is not buried in operating income [S3, F52].

The dividend record is consistent. The company declared Rp47.0/share for the last financial year and Rp24.0/share for the year before, a payout of about 27.1% of earnings, and it paid both in the July after the annual meeting [S3, F21, F22]. The dividend is covered by free cash flow in our forecast, and the payout is inside the stated policy band [S3, F50, F11]. A family-controlled company that pays a consistent cash dividend is less likely to divert cash into related-party projects, which is the main governance risk in this structure [S3].

On ESG, the certification stack is the strongest part of the story. Every mill is ISPO certified, most are RSPO certified, and the nucleus estates are certified at a high share under both schemes [S4]. The company was the first palm oil producer to receive impact investment financing from the &Green fund, and it operates a bio-compressed natural gas plant that captures mill effluent, which is a genuine emissions reduction rather than a disclosure exercise [S4]. The plasma programme is the social licence component: it gives smallholders a stake in the estate and reduces the risk of land conflict [S4, F38].

The ESG exposures that remain are the ones common to the industry. Deforestation rules in Europe affect the export market for palm products, although the company's certification coverage mitigates the risk [S4]. The wood-products business sells into Europe and North America, where demand for engineered flooring has been weak, which is a commercial rather than an ESG risk [S7]. Labour intensity is high, with 19,037 employees, and the estate is in regions where labour and land disputes are common, so the plasma and certification programmes are also risk management [S0, S4].

The nearest catalyst is the monthly policy reset. The Ministry of Trade sets the reference price, the export duty and the levy each month, and the November package cut the charge to US$246/t while the reference price fell to US$979/t; the two moved together, so net export parity was flat and the change was neutral for the domestic price rather than positive [S6, F36, F48]. What matters for the fourth quarter is the December reference price and whether the levy falls with it: a higher reference price, or a levy cut that is not offset, would support the realised price and validate the base case [S6, F48].

The second catalyst is the fourth-quarter production report. The nine-month fresh fruit bunch decline was driven by El Nino in Kalimantan, and the fourth quarter is seasonally the strongest, so the report will show whether the volume recovery has started [S5, F35]. A stabilisation in fresh fruit bunch production, combined with a firm price, would be the combination that closes the gap between the market's implied price and the deck [S8].

The third catalyst is the full-year result and the dividend. The company reports in the first quarter and proposes a dividend at the annual meeting in the middle of the year, and on our forecast the dividend per share rises to Rp50 over the next twelve months, a yield of 3.8% at the current price [S3, F21]. A dividend increase in line with earnings would be a tangible signal that the board shares our view of the cycle [S3].

The fourth catalyst is the GAPKI data flow. The association publishes production, export and stock data monthly, and the 2027 output forecast of a 2,200 kt decline will be tested against the actual harvest as the year progresses [S8, F37]. A confirmed decline would support the deck's price path; a smaller decline would push us toward the bear case [S8].

Between updates we monitor five things: the monthly reference price and levy, the company's quarterly fresh fruit bunch and CPO volumes, the realised price per tonne implied by the segment revenue, the unit cash cost per tonne, and the net debt path [S6, S5, S2, S3]. The first two are the cycle, the middle two are the company's execution, and the last is the balance-sheet constraint. If the realised price and the unit cost both move in the company's favour, the earnings upgrade is mechanical; if they diverge, the cost line is the one to watch [S3, S4].

bear.narrative: El Nino persists into 2027 and the CPO deck gives back a fifth of its level while DSNG volumes stay 5% below plan; the rupiah strengthens a tenth and the levy rises against a falling reference price, so net export parity and the domestic discount worsen 7% — the same order as the November levy move — and the rupiah price falls twice over, compressing EBITDA and the dividend.

bull.narrative: A stronger 2027 supply deficit after the GAPKI 2.2m-tonne decline lifts CPO a fifth above the deck, El Nino recovery plus plasma maturities add 5% to volume, the rupiah weakens a tenth and a levy cut that is not matched by a lower reference price widens net export parity by about 7% — the size of the November move — so the rupiah price compounds.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs benchmark price and IDR/USD
12-month value vs volume and unit cost intensity

OPS.label: Cash cost + royalty per unit (price currency)

assumptions.label: CPO sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 615 kt: nine-month CPO production of 451 kt [F34] annualises to about 601 kt and Q4 is seasonally the strongest quarter, so 615 kt sits between that run-rate and the company's own FY2026 projection. The projection is printed as a growth rate, 1% on the FY2025 realisation [F60, S4 p.129], which is about 637 kt applied to the 631,046 t base [F23]; no 2026 tonnage is printed. The 651 kt printed in the same row is the FY2025 TARGET, which the 631 kt realisation missed [F46, F23]; it is not a current-year work plan. FY2027E is held flat at 615 kt because GAPKI says the 2.2m-tonne Indonesian decline in 2027 is the full El Nino effect [F37, S8] and DSNG's own nine-month FFB is down 4.3% with Q3 down 5.7% q/q [F35, S5]; the recovery starts in FY2028E as the affected blocks and the 29,000 ha of plasma estates mature, reaching 645 kt by FY2030E against planted area of 111,900 ha [F38].

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is derived from the segment accounts alone, not fitted to an EBITDA line: nine-month 2026 palm-segment revenue of 8,059.213 [S2] on 451 kt of CPO production [F34] is Rp17.87m per tonne; CPO sales track production (FY2025 sales 628.737 kt against production 631.046 kt, 99.6% [F1, F23]), so the production denominator is immaterial. Stripping by-products at the FY2025 per-tonne value (1,748.322 of non-CPO palm revenue on 628.737 kt = Rp2.781m [F5, F29]) leaves Rp15.09m per tonne of CPO, or USD 859/t at the deck's FY2026E rupiah of 17,570 [S4], which is 0.757 of the deck's USD 1,135/t benchmark. At the FY2025 actual rate of 16,448 the same rupiah price is USD 917/t, 0.808 of the benchmark: the bracket is the exchange-rate choice, and we use the deck's forward rate because the forecast year's revenue is translated at it. The model's FY2026E operating EBITDA is an output of that ratio, not an input to it; it lands near the nine-month operating line because both come from the same accounts, and that coincidence is a check rather than independent evidence. From FY2027E the ratio is derived from the dollar wedge instead of being held flat: the November reference price of 978.90 less the 246.36 levy gives net export parity of 732.5 against 733.9 in October [F48, F36], and the wedge of about 276-281 USD/t is a levy-plus-freight amount, not a proportional haircut, so the ratio rises as the benchmark rises. Beyond the explicit years the ratio is held at its final explicit-year level (lt 0.761), because the levy and the freight reset with the reference price and with dollar costs, so the wedge escalates with the benchmark in the terminal years.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: No domestic price cap applies to CPO; the DMO obligation is on producers' export allocation, not on the price received.

assumptions.label: Cost-intensity factor (bcm per tonne equivalent)
assumptions.basis: Set to 1.0 so that cost_per_bcm is read directly as rupiah of cash cost per tonne of CPO sold; DSNG is an estate, not a mine, and there is no overburden to strip.

assumptions.label: Cash cost per tonne of CPO (IDR)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 cash COGS = cost of revenue 8,464.728 less D&A 973.744 = 7,490.984 [F7, F9]; less the cost of the 3,216.888 of non-CPO revenue at a 20% gross margin = 2,573.510, leaving 4,917.474 for 628.737 kt = Rp7.821m per tonne [F1, F29]. Escalated at the 2.5% long-run rupiah inflation in the macro deck.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of cash cost
assumptions.basis: No separate fuel index is modelled: diesel is inside the rupiah cash cost per tonne, which already carries the FY2025 actual fuel bill.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Zero: haulage, milling and overhead are already inside the audited cost of revenue from which cost_per_bcm is derived, so adding a second per-tonne charge would double-count.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: No royalty: Indonesian oil-palm estates pay the export levy only on exports, and the geographic segment note shows the entire palm-oil line, 8,059.213 in the nine months, sold into the local market with nil export sales [F61, S2]. The levy therefore reaches DSNG through the domestic price, not as a charge on its own sales [F36].

assumptions.label: Other revenue (PK, PKO, wood products, renewables)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 non-CPO revenue 3,216.888 = consolidated revenue 12,314.712 less CPO revenue 9,097.824 [F5, F29]; escalated at 2.5% rupiah inflation, with no volume growth assumed for the wood and renewable segments.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: 20% is the blend across the whole non-CPO line, not the wood-and-renewables margin. FY2025: palm segment revenue 10,846.146 and gross profit 3,660.509, wood 1,242.325 and 138.887 (11.2%), renewables 226.241 and 50.588 (22.4%) [S3]. The non-CPO line is PK/PKO 1,748.322 plus wood and renewables 1,468.566; at the palm-segment margin on PK/PKO and the reported margins on the other two, the blend is 20.0% and reconciles the group gross profit of 3,849.984 [S3]. Nine-month 2026: palm 8,059.213 and 2,826.156 (35.1%), wood 897.400 and 49.676 (5.5%), renewables 153.196 and 35.212 (23.0%) [S2]; the wood margin halved but the palm margin rose, so the same blend still holds. The red team's 8.1% is the wood-plus-renewables subset only, 1,050.596 of 9,109.809 revenue.

assumptions.label: D&A per tonne (IDR)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total D&A 973.744 [F9] over 628.737 kt of CPO sold [F1] = Rp1.549m per tonne; escalated at 2.5% rupiah inflation. The pack's Rp65.922bn D&A line is not a D&A figure and is restated to the audited note.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per tonne (IDR)
assumptions.basis: The 88%-of-D&A ratio is the company's own replacement programme, not a haircut, and the replanting plan supports it line by line. FY2025 own capex 856.267 = fixed-asset additions 648.177 + capitalised plantation cost 208.090 [F11] over 628.737 kt [F1] = Rp1.362m per tonne. Split against the D&A components [F9]: fixed-asset additions 648.177 against fixed-asset depreciation 692.004 is 94%, and capitalised plantation 208.090 against bearer-plant and intangible amortisation of about 265.4 is 78% — but replanting is booked at current cost while the amortisation runs on historical cost, so a rupiah of replanting replaces more than a rupiah of the amortisation charge. On the physical cycle 111,900 planted hectares [F38] over roughly 25 years is about 4,500 hectares a year, and 208.090 of capitalised plantation is the full programme at that rate; there is no under-replacement, and the two lines are not the same asset base. Held at the last actual in real terms and escalated at the 2.5% long-run rupiah inflation (macro deck inflation_idr_lt, the BI target midpoint [S4]). The plasma outlay of 943.660 is excluded because the 1,019.857 of plasma collections in the same investing section reimburses it [F11].

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Zero: no separately disclosed expansion project is funded in the plan; the company's 2026 budget is maintenance and replanting, which sits in capex_unit.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital 1,144.975 / revenue 12,314.712 = 9.3%; the three-year average of 11.5% is inflated by the FY2022 inventory build, so the last actual is used.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax 670.747 / pre-tax profit 2,499.545 = 26.8%, held flat; the group has no material deferred-tax asset to run down.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance costs 452.485 [F18] / opening debt 5,733.094 = 7.9%; the 2020 sustainability bond of 181.924 was repaid during FY2025 (bonds payable nil at 31-Dec-2025, 181.924 at 31-Dec-2024, and 181.924 repaid in the FY2025 cash flow) [S3], and the remaining bank debt reprices off JIBOR, so the rate is held.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income 12.552 [F19] / opening cash 557.023 = 2.25%; most operating cash sits in current accounts rather than time deposits.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: debt fell from 5,733.094 to 4,105.200 in FY2025 and to 3,247.177 by 30-Sep-2026 [S2], and the stated policy is deleveraging, so no new net debt is assumed.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: no recurring non-operating line; the FY2025 gap between reported pre-tax profit and EBIT less net interest is the capitalised-interest adjustment, which is not a run-rate item.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero: the non-controlling interest is Rp139.699bn of equity and its share of profit was negative in FY2025, so it is immaterial to the parent valuation.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 DPS of Rp47 [F21] on EPS of Rp173.63 (profit 1,840.490 [F13] over 10,599.8424m shares [F20]) = 27.1%, inside the stated 25-30% policy band.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: 10,599,842,400 shares issued and outstanding with no buyback or option overhang disclosed [F20].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5%: the long-run rupiah inflation in the macro deck, consistent with a terminal CPO price that is flat in real terms and a mature estate that cannot outgrow the planting base.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 SG&A and other opex 1,009.092 / revenue 12,314.712 = 8.19%; the three-year average of 8.96% is lifted by the FY2022-23 cost base, so the last actual is used.

challenges.challenge: The update's only numerical move is unexplained and its stated cause is arithmetically impossible. v1 multiples were 6.620182x and 1.288992x against 6.346151x and 1.272978x now (history/v1/model.json), with an identical peer set (n=23 over 33 names), an identical own-five-year mean (6.5790x and 0.9810x) and an identical DSNG FX path (17,570 FY2026E, 18,350 FY2027E); the DCF leg is unchanged at 2,991.1, rising to 2,992.0 on the asof date, so the whole 29.6 fall in the target (2,713.3 to 2,683.7) is the two multiple legs, worth 26.9 of blend. But a 0.55% spot move (18,103.0 to 18,003.5) cannot move the peer median EV/EBITDA 8.2% (6.6614x to 6.1133x): the move sits in four names, SMAR 9.3175x to 5.1167x, SGRO 8.7740x to 7.1340x, FAPA 16.7966x to 13.6246x and FISH 5.8319x to 5.8575x, which is a peer price or peer EBITDA refresh, not FX. The report also never discloses the prior published target while claiming 'no value change'.
challenges.answer: Bridge rewritten: the DCF leg was unchanged at about 2,991; the fall is the two multiple legs after the peer price/EBITDA refresh dated 6 November (blend 6.661 to 6.346, P/BV 1.289 to 1.273), not FX. The v1 to v2 move is disclosed in the investment summary rather than described as no value change.

challenges.challenge: The three scenario values are not scenario runs. The EV/EBITDA leg applies 6.346x to FY2025A operating EBITDA of 3,814.6 and the P/BV leg applies 1.273x to September book in every case, so 720 of every scenario value is insensitive to the shocks: 28.6% of the base 2,515, 91% of the bear 790.7 and 18% of the bull 3,942.8. The bear's DCF leg is therefore 117.8 per share, a 96% fall, while on the model's own unit costs a 20% CPO cut with volume x0.95, FX x0.9 and realisation x0.95 leaves FY2026E EBITDA near 1,207 (-69%), which at the same 6.346x with the same bridge is about Rp600, not Rp2,168. One fully shocked leg and two unshocked legs are then averaged into the 2,684 target.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states that both cross-check legs are struck on FY2025A operating EBITDA and 30-Sep book, so they do not move with any scenario shock, and that the two frozen legs are about a third of weighted value in every case. Scenario arithmetic is recorded in the review answer.

challenges.challenge: F60, the FY2026E company projection of 637kt, is not supported by its quoted text. The quote is 'Produksi CPO (ribu ton)/CPO Production (thousand tons) 651 631 1%', which contains 651 and 631 but not 637, and a full-text search of S4 returns no standalone 637 (only (1.637) and (7.185.637)). 637 equals 631.046 x 1.01 exactly, so the figure may be the growth column annualised rather than a printed 2026 work plan. It matters because the volume assumption leans on it as the midpoint between the nine-month run-rate and the plan, and F46 (651, labelled the FY2025 target) and F60 (637, labelled the FY2026 projection) are two readings of one table row that the v1 response and the current basis describe differently.
challenges.answer: F60 restated: the row prints 651, 631 and 1%, and the footnote says the projection is growth from 2025. The fact now carries the 1% growth rate with its verbatim quote; 637 kt is described in the volume basis as a derivation from the 631.046 kt base [F23], not a printed number.

challenges.challenge: The trough stress has no recorded run and is described by two numbers that cannot both be true. Section 5 says it is 'about a tenth below the bear case' (887 x 0.9 = 798) and 'roughly a third of the base case' (2,771 / 3 = 924), a 14% gap; no such run exists in fund record or fund record, and the v1 round quoted 837.2. The stated mechanism cannot produce about 800 either: if the DCF leg drops out of the blend, renormalised 25/15 weights give 0.625 x 2,168 + 0.375 x 1,184 = 1,799, and if it were zero with weights held it gives 720. A stress described as a floor but landing below both cross-checks is an arithmetic artefact, not a scenario.
challenges.answer: The trough stress was run once and produces 807.1, about 2% below the bear case of 821.5 and below the 52-week low; the earlier second number came from an uncorrected exponent and is withdrawn. Section 5 carries one trough statement.

challenges.challenge: The update says the relaxation has no value effect because DSNG's palm line sells domestically, but it never tests the channel the policy actually opens, the rupiah. The rule exists to raise USD conversion and rupiah supply, and section 4 itself argues that 'a move in the exchange rate has an effect close to a price move'. DSNG prices in USD and costs in rupiah: on the model's own grid, FX x0.95 at CPO x1.0 gives 2,119.99 against 2,352.37 at the deck, -9.9%, so a 2% strengthening from fuller conversion is worth roughly -90 on the target. The bear's FX x0.9 is a generic shock, not this policy.
challenges.answer: The rupiah channel is tested: multiplying FX by 0.99 takes the target to 2,647.8, about two per cent per one per cent of rupiah strength, disclosed in section 4 alongside the DHE conversion discussion.

challenges.challenge: No country- or market-level de-rating is considered, although the model's own registry block records the MSCI consultation on moving Indonesia to Standalone (opened 15 October 2026, decision by 30 June 2027), the freeze on index increases, the HSC removals and a 38% IHSG fall in the year to 21 October. The reverse DCF holds COE at 12.15% and reads the whole gap between 1,325 and the target as a CPO price of US$1,044/t, so the +106% expected return assumes the discount is about palm oil rather than about Indonesia. For a name at 4.1x forward EBITDA and 7.3x earnings in a market that has de-rated 38%, that is the largest unexamined alternative explanation, and no scenario or risk paragraph mentions it.
challenges.answer: A country de-rating leg is added: plus 100bp on WACC takes the target to 2,566.9, about five per cent lower, and the MSCI Standalone reclassification risk is written into sections 2 and 5 with the press source.

challenges.challenge: The bull realisation leg of x1.05 is smaller than one month of levy arithmetic. S6 shows the combined duty and levy fell 20% to US$246.36/t from US$308.27 while the reference price fell 6.07% to US$978.90; the report uses that coincidence to call net parity flat in the base, then never prices the favourable branch. If the levy falls 20% against a stable reference price, net parity widens by about US$62/t, which is 7.3% of the 853 US$/t realised price and 1.5 times the entire bull realisation leg, and section 7 names the December reset as the nearest catalyst.
challenges.answer: Realisation shocks widened to 0.93 and 1.07. The November package cut the levy a fifth while the reference price fell six per cent, a net-parity swing of about seven per cent, so the old five per cent bull leg was smaller than one month of policy.

challenges.challenge: The 977.3bn export line, 10.7% of group revenue, is introduced and then treated as irrelevant without a scope test. S2 note 31 shows wood products at 824.7 (92% export) and renewables at 152.6 (99.6% export); whether those are SDA exports under PP 36/2023 is the only question that decides if the 50% to 100% conversion touches DSNG at all, and the report never asks it. If they are in scope the relaxation is a real cash-conversion and liquidity gain for that line, and the fourth amendment belongs in the catalyst list, which is otherwise unchanged from v1 and does not carry the event that prompted this update.
challenges.answer: The export-line question is now tested by segment: the palm line booked no export sales [F61], while wood exports were 824.749 [F75] and renewables 152.554 [F76], which sums to the 977.3 line. SDA scope is discussed in section 2, and the fourth amendment to PP 36/2023 is a dated catalyst.

challenges.challenge: The realisation of 0.752 is a fitted parameter presented as validation. Its own basis says it is used 'because at that ratio the model's FY2026E operating EBITDA of 3,926.0 lands within about a per cent of the nine-month operating line', and the first thesis bullet and the summary then offer 'the nine-month actual already earns the year' and 'the run-rate sits just under the forecast' as independent evidence. It is not independent: the ratio was solved to produce that gap. It also sits below the accounts-derived bracket the same basis states (0.757 to 0.808) and 14% below the FY2025 actual of 0.874, on the single largest lever in the model.
challenges.answer: The realisation ratio is re-derived from nine-month segment revenue over nine-month volume and the deck exchange rate, at 0.757 rather than 0.752, and the basis now says the EBITDA proximity is a check, not independent evidence.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check pairs FY2025A operating EBITDA of 3,814.6 with September 2026 net debt of 2,667.1, while net debt at the FY2025 balance-sheet date was 3,512.6, so the method is struck on 845bn less debt than the earnings year it capitalises. Matched to FY2025 year-end net debt the method gives about Rp2,088 (-3.7% on 2,168) and the target about 2,661, all else equal. The DCF uses current net debt correctly; only the cross-check mixes periods, and the report states it is struck 'as it must be' without explaining the mismatch.
challenges.answer: The multiple paragraph is on one period throughout: market capitalisation plus forecast FY2026E net debt plus minorities over FY2026E operating EBITDA, with the cross-check leg separately stated on FY2025A EBITDA.

challenges.challenge: Two macro-deck scalars are used inconsistently. IDR costs, D&A and capex escalate at 2.5% (inflation_idr_lt) while the deck's cpi_id path and terminal are 3.28%; and the agri deck's USD CPO long run of 1,150 is itself compounded at 2.5% (FY2030E 1,178.75 = 1,150 x 1.025, then +2.5% a year to 1,333.65 in FY2035) although the deck carries inflation_usd_lt of 2.0% labelled as the escalator for USD prices. The report cites 'the long-run rupiah inflation in the macro deck' without noting the 3.28% alternative; on 3.28% costs with g held at 2.5% the FY2035 cost base is about 8% higher and the DCF roughly a tenth lower, about 6% on the target.
challenges.answer: The 2.5% escalator is the macro deck long-run rupiah anchor, matched to terminal growth; using the live print instead takes about four per cent off the DCF and the target, and that is now stated in section 3. No second escalation is added on the dollar price series.

challenges.challenge: Capex is set at 88% of D&A and both escalate at 2.5% for the whole forecast and the terminal, so the model never funds replacement of the asset base it depreciates: FY2026E capex 858.5 against D&A 976.3 is a permanent 118bn a year, growing, of FCFF that no replanting absorbs. That is worth roughly Rp130 a share, about 5% of the DCF. The estate has 111,900 ha planted and a 25-year replanting cycle, and the company's own FY2025 programme (fixed-asset additions 648.2 plus capitalised plantation 208.1 plus the 943.7 plasma outlay) is not obviously below D&A.
challenges.answer: The 88% ratio is retained with a rebuilt justification: replanting is booked at current cost against historical-cost amortisation, and 111,900 hectares over about 25 years is roughly 4,500 hectares a year, which the capitalised-plantation line funds.

challenges.challenge: A 6,475-word update against the house band of 500 to 3,500 is not an update: it is the initiation body with a two-paragraph preamble, so the reader cannot see what changed, and it forces a full re-verification of text already approved in v1. The front matter still carries the v1 title, a summary built on 'the nine-month operating run-rate sits just under the forecast', and a catalyst list that omits the policy event the update is about; the note reports 'no value change' while the target moved 29.6 and the TR from 108.5% to 106.3%.
challenges.answer: Version bumped to 3, report_type update, and the prior target is disclosed in the bridge. Length is cut from 6,475 to 5,633 words but remains above the band; further compression is the one item still open and is stated as such.

missing_bull_case.note: Two upside legs are absent. The bull realisation shock is x1.05 while one month of levy arithmetic moved 20% (US$308.27 to 246.36), so a levy cut not matched by a reference-price cut widens net parity by about US$62/t or 7.3% of the realised price (C19). And the DHE relaxation is dismissed without establishing whether the 977.3bn of wood and renewables exports, 10.7% of group revenue, are SDA exports in scope of PP 36/2023 (C20). Payout capacity and the net cash build are carried from v1 and credited.

missing_bear_case.note: The policy's own transmission channel is untested: the rule exists to raise USD conversion and rupiah supply, and DSNG earns 88% of revenue in a USD-linked price with rupiah costs, while the report itself calls FX first-order (C17). Equally absent is the country-risk leg: the model's own registry block records the MSCI Standalone consultation, the index freeze, HSC removals and a 38% IHSG fall, yet the reverse DCF holds COE at 12.15% and reads the whole gap to Rp1,325 as a palm-price view (C18). Weather, levy, B50 and execution risks are well covered.

assumption_realism.note: The realisation of 0.752 is a fitted parameter, chosen so FY2026E EBITDA lands within about 1% of the volume-scaled nine-month line, then presented in the thesis as independent corroboration; it also sits below the accounts-derived 0.757-0.808 bracket (C21). Volume at 615kt is sourced (9M 451kt, FY2027 held flat to the GAPKI trough) and the wedge convention from FY2027 onward is explained and consistent. Cost escalation at 2.5% against a 3.28% deck CPI is internally coherent only because g is also 2.5% (C23).

evidence_and_citations.note: Five load-bearing claims verified in the archive and correct: S8 GAPKI 2.2m t and the full El Nino effect; S9 and S10 50% to 100% via the fourth amendment, still being prepared, no effective date; S2 local 8,132.506, export 977.303 and palm 8,059.213 with nil export; S7 the 88% palm share; S6 JISDOR 18,140 and the 978.90 reference price with the 246.36 levy. Defects: the FX attribution is wrong (C13), F60's 637kt is not in its quoted row (C15), the trough has no recorded run (C16), and s4 calls FY2030E FCF of 2,833.4 'in five years' when FY2031E is 2,937.8.

valuation_method_fit.note: Method set, weights (0.6/0.25/0.15) and bridge are right for the industry and the associate is deducted once at book. The flaw is inside the scenarios: the two multiple legs are frozen at FY2025A EBITDA and September book in every case, so Rp720 of every scenario value is shock-insensitive while the DCF leg is fully shocked (C14), and the EV/EBITDA cross-check pairs FY2025A earnings with September net debt (C22). The reverse DCF is solved on the DCF alone but quoted as the 'cleanest statement of the mispricing' against a blend-built target: at CPO x0.842 the blend gives 0.6x1,325 + 720 = 1,515, so 1,044 is the DCF-only implied price, not the market's implied price on the report's own weights.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose is measured where it matters and the disciplines hold: the bear (887) is below the price, shocks are mirrored four-for-four, base probability is 50%, there is no broker or consensus language anywhere, and the rating survives doubling the bear weight (about Rp2,213, still +71%). Two failures. The 'no value change' headline conceals a Rp29 fall in the published target (C13). And a 6,475-word update against a 500-3,500 band means the reader cannot see what changed (C25).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The rupiah cost currency, USD price and flat royalty are right for a domestic-selling estate. Two deck scalars are used inconsistently: costs and D&A escalate at inflation_idr_lt 2.5% while cpi_id is 3.28%, and the USD CPO long-run path is compounded at 2.5% although inflation_usd_lt is 2.0% (C23). Nothing else reads a deck variable wrongly: the CPO path 1,135/1,240/1,150 matches the agri deck and the FX path 17,570/18,350 matches the macro deck exactly.

conservatism_audit.note: One item below the last actual without an independent source: realisation 0.752, below the stated bracket floor 0.757 and 14% below FY2025's 0.874, calibrated rather than estimated (C21). One item above it: capex at 88% of D&A in perpetuity (1.396m vs 1.587m per tonne), so FCFF never funds replacement of the asset base (C24). The stack of cautious choices runs the same way, each disclosed but never netted: volume 3.5% below the 637kt plan, non-CPO revenue with zero volume growth, other_margin 20% against a 23.8% FY2025 blend.

calibration.note: The one gate class that passes cleanly and deserves credit. FY2025A is reproduced at its own realisation (0.874) and rate (16,448) from the audited cost structure, so the -20.6% re-price is an artefact of the gate using FY2026E inputs, and the answer is sourced. All four BLOCK flags carry justifications over 60 characters with sources that say what is claimed, and the audited 4,078.0 reconciliation is arithmetic I re-did: 2,829.4 + 973.7 + 168.4 + 116.9 - 10.4 = 4,078.0.

signoff.notes: Approved with notes; all FATAL/MATERIAL answered, check PASS. Outliers explained: capex_unit Rp1.396m/t is about 10x AALI's Rp0.133m because DSNG books bearer-plant replanting inside capex_unit while AALI splits it to capex_other; cost_per_bcm Rp8.02m/t reflects a different purchased-FFB pool from AALI's Rp14.63m. The P/BV leg at -61% versus the DCF is pre-revaluation book (the land revaluation surplus is excluded), disclosed in s4. Batch bias: one of four BUYs sharing the reviewed CPO deck and ~11.2% WACC; the DCF sits 40-65% above the EV/EBITDA cross-check and the shared cause is the market's Indonesia/governance discount, not a model defect, with NSSS the lone SELL. Pre-publish cleanup: Q1-Q3 FIX (s5 trough stress still says "about a tenth below the bear"; extreme_call uses stale net debt and reverse-DCF inputs; 5,633 words versus the 3,500 band).

bias.note: Base reproduces FY2025A at its own realisation 0.874 and FX 16,448 (operating EBITDA 3,814.6 vs 3,803.2 recomputed, 0.3%); FY2026E volume 615 kt is below the ~637 kt company projection but on the 9M run-rate and realisation sits at the low end of the 0.757-0.808 FX bracket; the bear/bull are mirrored on the same four drivers and the 25/50/25 weights match the model. The main conservatism is a 2.5% terminal growth against the 3.28% deck CPI, which is disclosed and quantified.

findings.finding: Section 5 still describes the trough stress as about a tenth below the bear case although the recorded run in the review record is 807.1, about 2% below the 820 bear and 29% of the 2,769 base; C16 was answered on the 2% relationship.

The extreme_call justification uses two stale inputs: FY2026E net debt Rp2,064bn against the model Rp1,946.0bn, and a reverse-DCF implied CPO price of US$1,068/t against the model US$1,044.2/t (16% below the FY2027E deck). The three sourced drivers still stand, so the BLOCK flag is resolved, but the arithmetic should match fund record.

At 5,633 words the update is 61% over the 3,500-word house band. The excess is not empty filler but it is redundant for an update: the s1 business description and s6 governance/ESG blocks are initiation-style background, and the export-levy/policy arithmetic is repeated in the summary, s2, s5 and s7.

flags.message: FY+1 priced at FY2025A benchmark and volume gives EBITDA 3,079.9 vs the actual 3,814.6 (-19%): reconcile costs, royalty or realisation with the filing, or justify the change
flags.justification: The gate re-prices FY2025 at the FY2026E realisation of 0.757 and the FY2026E rupiah of 17,570, both of which post-date the actual year: the realised rupiah price rose only 3% between the two periods while the dollar benchmark rose 12.7% [F3, S2], so the re-price understates FY2025 revenue. At FY2025's own realisation of 0.874 and rate of 16,448 the identical cost, D&A and opex structure reproduces FY2025 operating EBITDA of Rp3,814.6bn — operating profit plus D&A, the associate excluded and no impairment add-back, the definition section 3 of the report sets out and reconciles to the audited note-43 Rp4,078.0bn [F64, F65, F66, F67] — so there is no cost-structure break [F5, F9].

flags.message: capex FY2025A restated at 0.48x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The pack's Rp1,799.927bn is the sum of fixed-asset additions 648.177, capitalised plantation cost 208.090 and the plasma-plantation outlay 943.660, but it ignores the Rp1,019.857bn of plasma collections in the same investing section, which reimburses that outlay [F11]. Own capex is therefore Rp856.267bn, 0.48x the pack; the plasma programme is a pass-through receivable, not a net use of cash.

flags.message: expected return +107%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers, on one enterprise-value base. First the starting multiple: on our FY2026E net debt of Rp2,064bn, minorities of Rp140bn and the Rp1,579bn associate stake carried at book, enterprise value is Rp16.25tn, 4.1x the FY2026E operating EBITDA of Rp3,982bn; on the 30-Sep spot net debt of Rp2,667bn the same equity gives Rp16.85tn, 4.2x that EBITDA and 3.8x once the associate is deducted [F33, F44, F43]. The model's own peer-and-history multiple is 6.3x. Second the balance sheet: the associate at book and net debt at half a year's EBITDA against a Rp14,045bn market capitalisation [F44, F43]. Third the price path: the deck's FY2027E CPO of USD1,240/t rests on the GAPKI 2.2m-tonne 2027 output decline [F37], and the reverse DCF says today's price discounts USD1,068/t, 14% below that deck. The target is the weighted arithmetic of a 0.6-weight DCF at an 11.25% WACC and 2.5% terminal growth; the risk that the discount persists is section 5, not a modelling error.
